summary:
Orbit of Errors is an interactive aerospace engineering simulation game where players act as Chief Systems Engineer and Flight Director to fix history’s famous spaceflight failures and outperform original mission designs.   What We Developed
We built a 1280x720 tactical mission simulator modeling the complete spacecraft lifecycle. Players integrate 20 authentic hardware components across six subsystems (GNC/OBC, Thermal/Radiation, Comms, Propulsion, EPS, and Launch Vehicles), manage real-time flight telemetry under realistic physics (inverse-square solar drop-off, Delta-V, radiation upsets), and diagnose failures via an interactive 6-Gate Engineering Post-Mortem.   How It Addresses the Challenge
Instead of arcade flying, the game tackles aerospace systems engineering through real constraints. Players balance strict budgets, daily factory burn rates, and launch windows against payload mass and quality-assurance testing. By recreating real historical root causes—like Imperial-to-metric software mismatches and unshielded circuits—players must optimize flawed architectures to survive.   Why It Is Important
Every major space disaster began on the assembly floor long before ignition. Orbit of Errors makes complex engineering trade-offs tangible, teaching systems thinking and showing why rigorous testing and margin management are essential for planetary exploration.
details: Orbit of Errors (NASA EYES: Anomaly Engineering) is a spaceflight systems-engineering simulator where players configure eight spacecraft subsystems using real NASA/JPL planetary data, manage assembly budgets and launch windows, intervene live during historical anomalies like Apollo 13's O2 rupture or Mars Climate Orbiter's unit mismatch, and analyze outcomes via a 6-gate post-mortem with spline telemetry curves. By turning aerospace trade-offs—such as mass versus $\Delta v$, solar flux, radiation shielding, and QA schedules—into immediate root-cause diagnostics inside a zero-dependency 60 FPS desktop app, it connects spaceflight enthusiasm with real engineering discipline to show how unit standardization, safety margins, and rigorous testing prevent mission failures. Built in C++20/26 and GLSL 330 using Raylib, CMake, Ninja, GCC, and VS Code on Linux, the project creatively transforms historical NASA failures and "Rush QA" schedule risks into solvable live crises enhanced by CRT/bloom shaders, particle thrusters, and audio ducking, while balancing scientific realism with ~55-second mission pacing (2.5x time warp) and a responsive 1280×720 virtual HUD.
